title: Suleyman the Lawgiver
hookLine: the sultan remembered in Turkey for law and justice

cards: One sultan, two nicknames. In Europe he's called Suleyman the Magnificent, for the splendor of his court, his armies at the gates of Vienna, his fleets on the Mediterranean.
But in Turkey, people remember him by a different name, a quieter one: Kanuni. The lawgiver. Not the conqueror.
Not the magnificent. The man who wrote things down so that people would know what the rules were. What a ruler is remembered for at home can be very different from what neighbors notice.

teach.b: Kanun means law, and specifically the law a ruler issues. In the Ottoman Empire there were two streams of law flowing side by side.
One was the sharia, God's law as worked out by Muslim scholars from the Qur'an and the example of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. The sultan could not change it.
The other was kanun: the ruler's decrees on things the sharia left open, like land, taxes, the ranks of officials, the duties of provinces.

Suleyman's reign is remembered for gathering and organizing these decrees, so that a judge in a distant town and a peasant on his land could, at least in principle, know what was owed and what was fair.

Beside him stood the chief mufti, the scholar Ebussuud Efendi, who worked to show how the sultan's law fit within the sharia. Justice was the point. The Qur'an asks believers to hold to it even when it costs them.

teach.h: STAUNCH IN JUSTICE, EVEN AGAINST YOURSELF.
teach.b: In Pickthall's translation: "Be ye staunch in justice, witnesses for Allah, even though it be against yourselves." Suleyman wasn't only a lawmaker. He wrote poetry under a pen name, Muhibbi, the loving one.

teach.h: A POET, AND A FATHER'S DARKNESS.
teach.b: And his reign had its darkness too: he ordered the death of one of his own sons.
A lawgiver is not a saint, and the tradition remembers both. Still, the name that stuck at home is this one. Not the size of the empire.
The fairness of its rules. The lawgiver.

how: In Turkey, Suleyman is known as Kanuni, the Lawgiver, and Muslim scholars still distinguish between the sharia and the laws a ruler issues on matters the sharia leaves open.

games.why: Suleyman's reign gathered and organized kanun, and the chief mufti Ebussuud worked to show it fit within the sharia.

practice: Think of one rule you're in charge of, at home, at work, with your kids or with yourself: bedtime, screen time, who does the dishes. Ask one honest question: do I keep this rule the same for everyone, including me?
If you pray, you can ask for a fair heart.

wordCard.voice: Kanun. The ruler's law that Suleyman, Kanuni the lawgiver, organized beside the sharia, in the name of justice. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: law, rule; in Ottoman use, the law a ruler issues. Kanuni means the lawgiver.
